title: Single-Shot Fidelity Reveals Hard and Soft Limits: A Universal Yardstick for Photon-Number-Resolving Detectors
authors: Tetsuya Tsuruta, Akio Yoshizawa, Daiji Fukuda
abstract: Photon-number-resolving (PNR) detectors are essential for photonic quantum computing, where a single measurement outcome must reliably herald a specific quantum state. However, detector fidelity is conventionally evaluated using ensemble-averaged statistics obtained from many measurements, which can remain high even when individual photon-number assignments are frequently misidentified. Here we introduce a universal single-shot fidelity that directly quantifies the probability of correctly identifying a photon number in a single measurement. The framework combines an efficiency-based POVM with a resolution-driven confusion matrix derived from the detector response, allowing photon loss and photon-number misidentification to be treated separately and then recombined into a single operational metric. This distinction reveals two fundamentally different limitations. Detection-efficiency loss represents an unrecoverable hardware constraint, whereas resolution-driven misidentification can be reduced by introducing a rejection region, trading generation rate for confidence. Because the metric is defined independently of detector architecture, it enables direct comparison between energy-resolving detectors such as transition-edge sensors and multiplexed click-based detectors on the same footing. Applying the framework to calibration data from three distinct detector architectures, we demonstrate quantitative comparison across photon-number regimes relevant to both discrete-variable and continuous-variable photonic quantum computing. The resulting benchmark provides a common operational metric for evaluating photon-number-resolving detectors and connecting detector performance to photonic quantum-computing requirements.
summary: This paper introduces a novel single-shot fidelity metric to rigorously evaluate Photon-Number-Resolving (PNR) detectors. It overcomes the limitations of standard ensemble averaging by explicitly separating hardware efficiency loss from errors caused by finite energy resolution. The resulting metric allows for the first direct, quantitative comparison of diverse detector technologies for use in photonic quantum computing.
main_problem: Conventional fidelity metrics for Photon-Number-Resolving (PNR) detectors are insufficient because they fail to quantify single-shot misidentification errors arising from finite energy resolution.
main_result: The authors introduce a single-shot fidelity metric that separates hardware efficiency loss from resolution-driven misidentification, allowing for a universal, direct comparison across different detector types.
method: They combine an efficiency-based POVM with a resolution-driven confusion matrix to construct a single-shot measurement probability, $P_{ss}(n|k)$.
model_or_system: The study focuses on PNR detectors essential for photonic quantum computing, comparing architectures like Transition-Edge Sensors (TES) and SNSPDs.
key_observables: Single-shot fidelity ($F_k$), detection efficiency ($\eta$), and the resolution confusion matrix ($\mathbf{R}_{ab}$).
important_parameters: Photon number ($k$), detection efficiency ($\eta$), and the acceptance region ($	au$) used to define measurement boundaries.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the detector output retains a gradient of confidence about the true photon number, and Gaussian approximations are used for modeling detector responses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of the single-shot POVM, showing how the composition of efficiency and resolution matrices yields the final fidelity, and compare $F_k$ vs. $k$ for different detector types and operating regimes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the inadequacy of ensemble-averaged metrics, then develops the single-shot fidelity framework by composing the POVM and confusion matrix, and finally applies this framework to compare multiple real-world detector architectures.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, quantitative benchmark for quantum hardware, directly linking fundamental detector physics (resolution) to the operational requirements of quantum computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A concrete example of the resolution confusion matrix Rab, cen- tered on a = 3. The horizontal axis is the true photon number and the vertical axis is the reported photon number. The diagonal element R33 car- ries the dominant weight, with leakage into neighboring photon numbers, R32 and R34, appearing as off-diagonal elements. This matrix represents single-shot misidentification arising from finite energy resolution alone.

Figure 2: Construction of the single-shot POVM. Shown here for illustra- tion is a 1550 nm photon measurement with detection efficiency 97 % and resolution 0.6 eV. Composing the conventional POVM Pexp(m|k), which in- cludes only the detection efficiency (η) and small residual label errors (left), with the resolution confusion matrix Rmn defined in Fig. 1 (center), yields the single-shot POVM Pss(n|k) = P m Pexp(m|k)Rmn (right), which carries single-shot misidentification due to the overlap of neighboring peaks as off- diagonal elements.

Figure 3: Dependence of single-shot fidelity Fk on the heralded photon number k, for a 1550 nm photon measurement. Horizontal axis: heralded photon number k; vertical axis: Fk (linear scale). (a) Energy resolution fixed, detection efficiency η varied (e.g., η = 1.0, 0.99, 0.95, 0.90). (b) De- tection efficiency fixed at η = 1, energy resolution FWHM varied over 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60 eV. Overlaying the two series shows that detec- tion efficiency and resolution each independently degrade Fk.

Figure 4: Schematic of the accept region. For the confusion matrix centered on a = 3, the accept regions for τ = 1 (no rejection, the ordinary equal- likelihood boundary) and for τ > 1 are shown side by side. For τ > 1, reject bands appear near the boundaries with neighboring peaks; the figure shows both the contraction of the accept region toward the center and the fraction of events falling into the reject bands.

Figure 5: Trade-off between fidelity and generation rate via the accept re- gion. For a fixed target photon number n, sweeping the threshold τ from 1 to τ ∗traces out the yield Yn(τ) (horizontal axis, corresponding to the generation rate sacrificed) against the conditional fidelity Cn(τ) (vertical axis). Curves are shown for several values of energy resolution. Each curve terminates at the optimum point τ ∗beyond which raising τ no longer helps (star). Detectors with better resolution reach higher Cn, and sacrifice less generation rate to reach a given Cn.
